lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: Prove It
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 2, Session 3
lesson.footer: Persuasive Writing | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 2 Session 3

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LA02 moving beyond bare assertions by using authoritative sources; VC2E5LY09 evaluating information and ideas; VC2E5LY10 creating persuasive texts with elaborated ideas
plan.shape: sort, match, write: name the kinds of evidence, match fact cards to claims, then write a paragraph that proves it, because students' arguments are mostly opinion until they learn to pick and cite proof
plan.criticalFeature: evidence must match the claim and come from someone who would know
decisionPoints: the What kind of evidence? round
the choice check: which evidence matches the claim?
the exit board: the best evidence for a new claim
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Today is Prove it.
plan.catchUp: Missed earlier sessions? Say the anchor, give the Arctic Fact Cards and the claim Polar bears need our help. They write today's paragraph on that claim.

studentTools: Arctic Fact Cards, one set per pair
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: Four evidence types: fact, statistic, expert, example

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: name the evidence, match it, say who said it, then write a Prove it paragraph.
resources.title: Prove It
resources.subtitle: Proof must match the claim and come from someone who would know.

example.prompt: 'A vet says most dog bites happen at home.'
steps: Is it a person who knows?

items.prompt: Write the kind of evidence: fact, statistic, expert or example.
rows: Our survey: 19 of 24 kids want a garden.
A dentist says sugar damages teeth.
Last week a magpie swooped my brother.
answers: Our survey: 19 of 24 kids want a garden.
A dentist says sugar damages teeth.
Last week a magpie swooped my brother.

example.prompt: Claim: our oval needs drains. Evidence: it floods every winter.
steps: Who said it? Would they know?
example.answer: It matches: both are about water on the oval.

items.prompt: Claim: our school needs more bike racks. Which proof matches?
items.explain: It is about racks at our school, with numbers someone counted.

items.prompt: Zara wrote this proof. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Scientists say polar bears are in danger.
items.answer: Which scientists? Fix: According to the IUCN Red List, polar bears are listed as Vulnerable.

steps: Add who they are, between commas
example.answer: According to NASA, the US space agency, summer sea ice is shrinking about 12 percent a decade.

items.prompt: Use the Arctic Fact Cards. Write an According to sentence for each card.
answers: According to Polar Bears International, a group that studies bears, bears hunt seals from the ice.
According to Polar Bears International, some bears go months without eating when the ice melts.
According to the CSIRO, Australia's science agency, burning coal, oil and gas warms the planet.

example.prompt: Claim: polar bears need our help.
example.answer: Polar bears need our help. According to NASA, ... This means ...

items.prompt: Write a claim-prove-sell paragraph for your issue, with real evidence and who said it.
items.answer: A claim, a sourced fact, a This means sentence and a sell.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: judge sources, then turn weak proof into strong proof.
resources.title: Source Judge
resources.subtitle: Not every source deserves your trust.

example.prompt: Source: a cruise company's ad saying the Arctic is 'unspoiled'.
example.answer: Low: they want to sell cruises.

items.prompt: Rate each source high or low, and say why.
rows: A book by a polar bear scientist
An ad for an Arctic cruise
answers: A book by a polar bear scientist
An ad for an Arctic cruise

example.prompt: Weak: lots of people think bears are in trouble.
steps: Who? How many? How do they know?
Find a fact with a source
example.answer: Strong: The IUCN Red List lists polar bears as Vulnerable.

items.prompt: Write two proof sentences for the same claim: one weak, one strong. Then explain what makes the strong one strong.
items.answer: A weak and a strong version, and an explanation naming the source.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: Supported option: picture-clue choices, a first According to done and a paragraph frame.
resources.title: Prove It Helper
resources.subtitle: Proof is a fact, a number, an expert or an example.

items.prompt: A vet says dogs need walks.
items.hint: Is it a person who knows?

example.answer: According to NASA, sea ice is shrinking.

items.prompt: Use a fact card. Finish each sentence.
rows: According to NASA, sea ice is shrinking.
answers: According to NASA, sea ice is shrinking.
According to the IUCN, polar bears are Vulnerable.
According to Polar Bears International, bears hunt from the ice.
items.hint: The first one is done for you.

example.answer: Polar bears need help. According to NASA, sea ice is shrinking. This means bears can't hunt.

items.prompt: Finish: Polar bears need our help. According to ___, ___. This means ___.
items.answer: A claim, a sourced fact and why it matters.

resources.label: Arctic Fact Cards
resources.description: Eight real facts with their sources, numbered for the matching round and the You Do. One set per pair.
resources.title: Arctic Fact Cards
resources.subtitle: Real facts with their sources. Choose the card that proves your claim.

cards.text: 1. Polar bears hunt seals from the sea ice. Without ice, they cannot reach their food. (Polar Bears International)
2. Arctic summer sea ice is shrinking by about 12 percent every ten years. (NASA)
3. There are about 26,000 polar bears left in the wild. (IUCN estimate)
4. Polar bears are listed as Vulnerable to extinction. (IUCN Red List)
5. In 2011, scientists tracked a polar bear that swam for nine days and about 687 km. (US Geological Survey)
6. When the ice melts in summer, some polar bears go months without eating. (Polar Bears International)
7. Burning coal, oil and gas releases gases that trap heat and warm the planet. (CSIRO)
8. Australia has warmed by about 1.5 degrees since 1910. (CSIRO and Bureau of Meteorology)

resources.tip: Stretch: which card would a doubter find hardest to argue with? Why?

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today we stop saying trust me and start proving it.

Print one Arctic Fact Cards sheet per pair. Then the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it. Every fact card is real, with its source.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to back up a claim with strong evidence.
successCriteria: I can name four kinds of evidence.
I can choose evidence that fits my claim, from someone who would know.
I can say who my source is, with extra detail between commas.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Today is Prove it. The magnifier.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Naming the kinds of evidence is where we start.
Choosing evidence that matches is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 naming evidence types is reachable for all; SC2 choosing matching, trustworthy evidence is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 the appositive is the stretch (Term 3 Week 5 retrieval).

slides.title: Who would you believe?
lines: Claim: polar bears are in danger.
Said by: a stranger online, a polar bear scientist, or your cousin?

notes.answer: the scientist - they study it, so they would know
beats: SAY: Three people tell you polar bears are in danger.
Same claim. Who do you believe most?
ASK: Who would you believe? 1 stranger, 2 scientist, 3 cousin.
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, 1, 2 or 3... show me.
EXPECT: 2
ASK: Why the scientist?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: they study bears; they have proof; it's their job
SAY: Who says it matters. Today we choose proof from people who would know.
trap: trusting the cousin because they're family.
Fix: ask how would your cousin know? Student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Launch sets up the second half of the critical feature: from someone who would know. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: Facts, numbers, expert words or examples that show a claim is true.
slides.example: Claim: bears are hungry. Evidence: they go months without eating.

notes.answer: facts, numbers, expert words or examples that show a claim is true
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Evidence. Say it with me. Evidence.
SAY: Evidence shows your claim is true.
Four kinds: a fact, a statistic, an expert, an example.
ASK: Name the four kinds to your partner without looking.
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: fact, statistic, expert, example
trap: thinking a strong opinion is evidence.
Fix: ask how do we know it's true? Student names a fact or source.
notes.prep: The word the session runs on, with the four kinds named once.

slides.title: Pick proof that fits
lines: Claim: polar bears are running out of ice.
Best proof: card 2, a NASA statistic.
According to NASA, the US space agency, summer sea ice is shrinking fast.

notes.answer: match the proof to the exact claim, then say who it comes from
beats: POINT to the claim.
SAY: My claim is about ice. So my proof must be about ice.
POINT to card 2.
SAY: Card 3 is about bear numbers. True, but not about ice.
Card 2 is about ice, from NASA.
POINT to the sentence.
SAY: I say who, plus a few words on who they are, between commas.
ASK: What are the extra words between my commas?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: the US space agency
trap: grabbing the most shocking fact, even if it's about something else.
Fix: student underlines the key word in the claim, finds it on the card.
notes.stretch: Add a second card that proves the same claim.
notes.help: Underline the topic word in the claim, then find it on a card.
notes.prep: The model. Critical feature: evidence must match the claim and come from someone who would know. Near-miss: card 3, true but off-topic.
notes.sources: SOURCES: NASA Vital Signs (Arctic sea ice minimum, about 12 percent per decade); IUCN polar bear estimate.

slides.title: What kind of evidence?
slides.pivot: ask: is it a number, a person, a story, or a fact?
slides.followUp: cold call one student: which words told you?

items.text: Bees pollinate many of the crops we eat.
Our class survey found 21 of 26 students walk or ride to school.
A marine biologist explains that turtles often swallow plastic bags.
Last summer, a thirsty koala wandered into our school yard.
The Bureau of Meteorology reports Australia has warmed about 1.5 degrees since 1910.
items.say: Both! A statistic from an expert source. That's the strongest kind. Tick or fix.

trap: calling any sentence with a number a fact, not a statistic.
Fix: ask is there a number? Then it's a statistic. Student re-votes.
notes.stretch: Rank the five from strongest to weakest.
notes.help: Look for a number first, then a person, then a story.
notes.prep: Guided sort on SC1. The last item is the edge case: a statistic from an expert. SC1.

slides.title: Which evidence matches the claim best?
slides.prompt: Claim: our school needs more water fountains.

options.text: Polar bears are listed as Vulnerable to extinction.
options.misconception: true, but it doesn't match this claim

options.text: In our survey, 18 of 25 students were thirsty after lunch play.
My friend reckons cold water is really nice to drink.
options.misconception: matches the topic but comes from someone who wouldn't know

notes.answer: B - it's about our school and our students, with numbers
beats: SAY: A new claim. Find the evidence that fits it.
ASK: Which evidence matches the claim best?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: what's wrong with A? It's true.
Less -> underline the claim's key words, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. Our school, our students, real numbers. It fits and we can trust it.
trap: pointing to A because it is a real, serious fact.
Fix: ask is it about water fountains? Student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Decision point before the card matching. Under 80% means the first two matching items are done together.

slides.title: Which card proves it?
slides.pivot: underline the key word in the claim, find it on a card
slides.followUp: cold call one board: who is the source on your card?

items.text: Claim: polar bears depend on the ice to eat.
Claim: melting ice forces bears into dangerous journeys.
Claim: what we do in Australia affects the Arctic too.
Claim: polar bears could disappear one day.
items.say: Card 4. Vulnerable to extinction is the official warning. Tick or fix.

say: Get your Arctic Fact Cards out with your partner.
Each claim needs one card. Write its number.
trap: choosing the most dramatic card every time.
Fix: student reads the claim's key word aloud and checks the card has it.
notes.stretch: Name a second card that could also work.
notes.help: Lay the cards in a row; read each claim's key word first.
notes.prep: Guided matching with the fact cards. SC2.

slides.title: Write a Prove it paragraph
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet. Finish with a Prove it paragraph for your issue.
slides.visualLabel: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it.

beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Use your own issue.
Need proof? Use a fact card, or ask me for a source.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Ask: does your proof match your claim? Who said it?
TIME 15 minutes. At 12, two students read their According to sentence.
trap: proof without a source: Scientists say...
Fix: ask which scientists? Student names the organisation from the card.
notes.stretch: Extension: judge sources, then turn weak proof into strong proof.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: picture-clue choices, a first According to done, a frame.
notes.prep: Independent application. The anchor's three moves in one paragraph, used again in Week 4 drafting. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in a claim-prove-sell paragraph with a sourced fact

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Claim: our school should plant more shade trees.
A: Trees are pretty.  B: Cancer Council says shade protects kids from UV.  C: My dad likes trees.
Write the best letter and why.

notes.answer: B - it matches the claim and comes from health experts
beats: SAY: A new claim about our school. Choose the best proof.
ASK: Write the letter of the best proof and one reason.
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: B, because Cancer Council are experts on sun safety
RECORD who chooses A or C. Tomorrow's small group.
trap: choosing A because trees are pretty is true.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new claim. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Read your According to sentence to your partner. Would a doubter believe it?

notes.answer: open - listen for a named source that would know
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can choose evidence that fits?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Read your According to sentence. Would a doubter believe it?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: yes, it says NASA
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. Students keep the fact cards in their books for drafting. SC2.
